title: MA9-07061
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, his spouse, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX XXXXX, their son, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, and their daughter, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX XXXXX, citizens of Mexico, are claiming refugee protection in Canada under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

Pursuant to subsection 167(2) of the IRPA and rule 15 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules, the principal claimant, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX, confirmed during his hearing that he would assume the role of designated representative for his minor daughter, XXXXX XXXX XXXXX XXXXX.
In light of the copies of the claimants' passports filed in evidence,1 the panel is satisfied as to their identities.
The principal claimant alleged the following.
On XXXX, 2008, two men, members of the Mara Salvatrucha, broke into the family home and threatened and forcibly confined the claimant and his family.
On XXXX, 2008, he managed to escape the family home and take refuge at his uncle's home in Tlaxcala.

He did not file a complaint with the police because he feared the Mara Salvatrucha had infiltrated the Mexican police and because the next door neighbours (XXXX XXXX) had been killed by the Mara Salvatrucha after they filed a police report against them.
On XXXX, 2008, he left Mexico to travel to Canada and claim refugee protection.
On XXXX, 2008, the principal claimant was joined by his wife and children in Canada to claim refugee protection.

Having reviewed all of the testimonial and documentary evidence, the panel determines that the claimant failed to discharge his burden of establishing a "serious possibility of persecution" should he return to Mexico. The claims for refugee protection filed by his wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, their son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX are also rejected, as they are based on the same facts as the claim filed by the principal claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX. The panel determines that the principal claimant, his wife, and their children also failed to establish that, on a balance of probabilities, they are "persons in need of protection."

The panel is of the opinion that no evidence was produced by the claimant to establish a nexus between his fear and one of the five Convention grounds; therefore section 96 of the IRPA does not apply.

The claimant's evidence did not implicate the Mexican state or one of its agents as an agent of persecution. As a result, the panel concludes that the claim cannot be considered under paragraph 97(1)(a) of the IRPA.
The panel is of the opinion that the claimant's claim for refugee protection also cannot be allowed under paragraph 97(1)(b) of the IRPA, for the following reasons.

Having heard the testimony and analyzed all the evidence, the panel concludes that the principal claimant and the members of his family were victims of generalized crime and that they could take refuge elsewhere in Mexico without being threatened or attacked by their alleged assailants.

During his hearing, the claimant's testimony was spontaneous and contained no contradictions. He alleged that he and his family were threatened and forcibly confined by two members of the Mara Salvatrucha. When asked why these two men had broken into their family home, the claimant answered that they had simply decided to take possession of his home and that they thought the home was well-suited to their activities. When asked whether he had recognized his assailants, the claimant answered that, at first, there were two armed men with distinctive Mara Salvatrucha tattoos. Afterwards, some other men joined them in the claimant's home. When asked whether he owned the house, the claimant answered that he did not; he was renting it. When asked whether he was personally targeted by his assailants or whether it was his house that interested them, the claimant answered that he had been personally targeted because of his home and its particular features. Thus, although the claimant stated that he was personally targeted, the panel cannot agree with this statement. On the contrary, according to his testimony, the claimant's assailants had just one intention: to take illegal possession of his home in order to carry out criminal activities. The claimant was not the owner of this home; he had been a tenant for several years. The panel is of the opinion that it is reasonable to believe that the identities of the tenants of this home was of little significance to the assailants. It was rather, as stated by the claimant, the location of the home and its particular features that were important to the assailants.

The panel finds the principal claimant to be credible. However, the panel cannot conclude that he and his family were personally targeted by their assailants. In this case, it was not the individuals who were personally targeted, but rather the home they occupied. In support of this conclusion, the claimant stated at his hearing that he had not been threatened or attacked by the Mara Salvatrucha when he went to his uncle's home in XXXX with his family. In addition, according to the claimant, his father-in-law (father of his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX) owns the home and allegedly was not threatened or attacked by the Mara Salvatrucha following the events of XXXX 2008. His father-in-law did not demand that the Mara Salvatrucha leave the home and did not file a complaint with the police, for fear of reprisals.

During his testimony at the hearing, the claimant stated that his assailants are members of the Mara Salvatrucha, a criminal organization. When asked about the reasons that could have led these criminals to search for him throughout Mexico and put so much effort into tracking him down and threatening him, the claimant answered that they certainly had ties with other criminal organizations. The panel is of the opinion that it is implausible that criminals whose obvious objectives were to possess and occupy the claimant's home would put so much effort into tracking him down throughout Mexico. The claimant failed to persuade the panel on this issue. The panel is of the opinion that it is more likely that the claimant's assailants have no intention of tracking him and his family down or pursuing them. Not only have more than two years elapsed since the last incident, but the claimant also filed no complaint with the police and did not submit any evidence indicating that his assailants tried to find him or track him down following the incident of XXXX 2008. In addition, the claimant was not the owner of the home; he had been renting this home from his father-in-law for a few years. Accordingly, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant and his family were victims of generalized crime and that they were not personally targeted by their assailants, as previously mentioned. It was rather their house that was targeted.

In addition, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant could seek refuge elsewhere in Mexico. During his hearing, the claimant was asked what he would fear if he had to return to live elsewhere in Mexico, in the states of Yucatán or Zacatecas, the claimant answered that he could not go to either of these states because the Mara Salvatrucha are there and they could easily track him down. When confronted with the documentary evidence2 indicating that the Mara Salvatrucha are not active throughout Mexico and that they are not present or not active in the states of Yucatán and Zacatecas, the claimant stated that he was not aware of that fact, but that he believes the Mara Salvatrucha-even though they are not present in certain states of Mexico-have close ties with other criminal organizations. The panel is not satisfied with this explanation. The panel finds it implausible that the members of this group (Mara Salvatrucha) would try to track down the claimant in the states of Yucatán or Zacatecas, if he moved to one of these states, since in all likelihood, they are not active there. In addition, this group showed no interest in tracking down the claimant and his family, even through other criminal groups, when they were in XXXX, about 45 minutes from their home in XXXX. Once again, the panel is of the opinion that the assailants achieved their goal of taking possession and occupying the claimant's home, not of threatening or assaulting the claimant and his family. Therefore, despite the opportunity the panel gave the claimant to support his evidence, he did not give a reason why it would be unreasonable, as set out in the case law,3 to travel to the states of Yucatán or Zacatecas to seek refuge there. He also failed to submit actual and concrete evidence of conditions that would subject him to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant could relocate to another city in Mexico. During his hearing, the claimant stated that he fears that his assailants will find him. According to the claimant's testimony, the last time he saw or was threatened by the two assailants dates back to XXXX 2008, over two years ago. Since XXXX 2008, the claimant has not heard any news of his assailants, apart from the fact that they are still occupying the home rented by the claimant and his family.

The panel is of the opinion that the claimant failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that relocating to another part of Mexico, specifically the states of Yucatán or Zacatecas, would cause him to fear for his life. The claimant's main argument is that the alleged assailants are members of the Mara Salvatrucha criminal group and that they would be able to find him throughout Mexico. The panel is of the opinion that it is unlikely that the two assailants would feel the need to track down and pursue the claimant elsewhere in Mexico. These two criminals have not been heard from since XXXX 2008. According to the claimant's testimony, the assailants' goal was to take possession and occupancy of their family home, because it has several features that meet the needs of this criminal group. The panel is not prepared to accept that these two criminals could be tempted to travel throughout Mexico to find the claimant. Accordingly, the claimant failed to present evidence that his alleged assailants would have any interest in pursuing him or searching for him. It is implausible that the claimant would be of such interest to the alleged assailants that they would try to track him down in Mexico, specifically in the states of Yucatán or Zacatecas.

Therefore, the panel concludes that it is not objectively unreasonable to believe or unduly harsh to expect that the claimant could relocate to the states of Yucatán or Zacatecas. The claimant stated that he would have no problem returning to Mexico and relocating to one of these states, apart from his expressed fear of the members of this criminal organization (Mara Salvatrucha).

As stated by the Honourable Justice Lagacé in Ramirez: ... the burden of proof regarding an internal flight alternative rests on the claimant. Thus, the claimant had to establish either that it would be unreasonable for him to seek refuge in another part of the country or that there were, in fact, conditions preventing him from relocating elsewhere ...4 In Palacios, Justice Shore noted what the case law has upheld many times: It is settled law that in matters concerning internal flight alternatives the burden of proof is on the applicant: ... Therefore, the refugee claimant must demonstrate that it would be unreasonable for him or her to seek refuge in a different part of the country.5 In Thirunavukkarasu,6 the Court of Appeal established that the burden is on the claimant to demonstrate why, on a balance of probabilities, he would face a risk of persecution in a part of the country where there is an internal flight alternative.

In this case, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant failed to discharge his burden of proof as required in the case law7 and concludes that there is an internal flight alternative for him in the states of Yucatán or Zacatecas.

Accordingly, the panel determines that the principal claimant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, his wife, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, their son, XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, are not "Convention refugees" or "persons in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

For these reasons, their claims for refugee protection are rejected.
